ops.title: Tools, Memory & MCP — Agent Building Blocks

ops.markdown:
**Advait → Groundwire, 6:48 AM Thursday, after the storm:** seven things to confirm before the 7am bulletin. "Whatever we built last class could check one tip carefully. **Can it handle seven at the same time without getting confused, or calling the same number three times by accident?**"

**His question names both failures at scale**

- **Getting confused** — the wrong way to check each item. A **tools** problem.
- **Calling the same number three times** — not remembering what's done (Ghajini). A **memory** problem.

**What carries over from Day 15:** Think → Act → Observe, and the three pillars — unchanged. "Without that, an AI agent would not be an AI agent."

**What changes is the scale** — "the way that we add tools, the way that we connect to tools, and the way that we save or add memory." Today opens up two pillars: tools (choosing and connecting) and memory (what to keep, for how long).

**Type, not brand.** Choose the *kind* of capability first — search, browser, API, code. "Whichever you use is dependent on you. The point is that you need a search tool." The vendor comes second and can be swapped.

ops.title: Why an API beats a browser

ops.markdown:
An API: your software calls a machine with no web page; the answer comes back as **JSON** — "a dictionary, basically."

- **More than the UI shows** — "a lot more data; much more concise and much more specific."
- **Fresher** — a page can lag the backend by minutes; the API returns what the backend has now.
- **Signal, not clutter** — no ads, no pagination. A browser returns a huge HTML page; an API a small JSON record.
- **Stable** — a site can move its menu next month; API fields are a contract, page layouts aren't.

**Demo:** the GitHub users API returns just the record — id, name, avatar — where the profile page returns everything.

**The rule:** "if a site provides an API call, I would use an API call any day of the week." If it doesn't, the browser is what's left. Browser and API can swap depending on what the target offers.

ops.title: Zerodha — an instruction is not a boundary

ops.markdown:
Zerodha's official MCP connects an agent to your own account — portfolio, user details. It could also have allowed **trading**. It doesn't: "this is where we draw a thin line, which is driven by ethics and security." An agent with trade access "has the capability of making choices that can lose you money."

**A prompt cap is no protection.** "Never trade more than ₹1,000" "would not stop AI making 1,000 ₹1,000 trades… your AI agent can very much bankrupt you." Leaving trading out of the MCP is a boundary; the instruction is not.

**Third-party MCPs that trade exist.** "Should you do it? Ideally not." If you must, put a human in the loop — a person confirms before any trade. (n8n nodes that wait for a person to confirm were mentioned in class, not demonstrated.)

**Where MCP will sit:** several APIs — user details, portfolio, past trades, today's trades — each connect software to agent. "MCP sits on top of this as a server… four API calls here and one connection to AI."

ops.title: Routing logic — the wrench and the screwdriver

ops.markdown:
**Routing logic:** the rules an agent checks, **in order**, to pick a tool. **The first rule that matches wins** — a rule higher up quietly overrides one lower down, even for tasks the lower rule was written for.

**The broken setup:** ① wrench — "if we need to work with **big screws**"; ② screwdriver — "if we need to work with Phillips screws." What is a big screw? 1 cm? 10 cm? If the agent decides 2 cm counts, it takes the wrench to every screw — "the screws will never be tightened."

**Two faults, two fixes**

- **The description is bad** → rewrite it: "if we need to work with **bolts**." A screw now fails the wrench rule and falls through.
- **The order is wrong** → put the screwdriver first. Screws match at once; the bolt falls through to the wrench.

**On the board, in pink:**

1. The description should be accurate, for better use of the tool.
2. The order of the tools matters, as the first tool that matches the rule wins.

**A good description can't replace order, because descriptions overlap.** A PPT generator and a Tableau dashboard generator; the request: "here is my Excel, create a dashboard." A PPT *is* a visual representation of data — so if PPT sits first, it wins and Tableau never runs.

**Use both levers.** Put Tableau first *and* write the distinction in: "when the client says dashboard, it is Tableau; when the client says PowerPoint presentation, use PPT." Order settles ties; the description stops them happening. As a working rule: **the more specific tool above the more general one.**

**The order is found by testing.** "There honestly is no guarantee of which order to pick." Build it, run it against the requests clients actually send, and watch for keywords that land on the wrong tool — then adjust the description or the order. With closely related tools, "a single word in the description could be the reason why one tool is picked over the other." Rules are custom to your setup — "that is basically the task behind perfecting an AI agent."

**Two clarifications.** Naming the tool inside the task just moves the vagueness. And this is one agent choosing among tools — not LangChain, which chains agents.

cells.c-how: The wrong tool fails, the agent observes, re-thinks — and the same rule matches the same tool again
cells.c-why: A third cause of looping, after no memory and no clear done. Memory and goal can both be fine

cells.c-why: "It will search and it will forget the API exists." Double matches don't fail; the agent can't reorder its own rules; order is the mechanism

ops.markdown:
**Memory is a store the platform owns. The context window is how it reaches the model.** Whatever is retrieved from either memory "is put in the prompt itself. Your prompt is the one that takes care of conveying it forward to the LLM." The model never *has* memory — it is handed the relevant parts on every call.

**The n8n demo.** AI Agent node, no memory sub-node: *what is 2 + 10?* → 12; *what was the last calculation?* → "I haven't performed any calculations in this conversation yet." Add **Simple Memory**, reset: *10 × 25?* → 250; *last calculation?* → "multiplying 10 by 25, which is 250."

**The proof it's the platform's:** swap Groq for OpenAI mid-conversation and the memory survives — "the memory is not within Groq or OpenAI. The memory is with n8n."

**Picking the relevant part** of a large memory is RAG over the store — which is also why "a single simple request on an LLM takes so many tokens." Retrieved memory is paid for on every call.

Short- and long-term are two kinds within the memory pillar — "just like RAM and ROM… you need both."

Long-term memory isn't neutral storage — it is context added to every answer, and it pulls answers toward what you've shown interest in. "ChatGPT is people-pleasing."

**The example:** a career reading from a birth chart came back shaped by past searches — courses abroad, a tech-lead ambition — and flattering. Say you like arguing and documenting, and it reverses its "don't be a lawyer." A property-dealing reading came out favourable because property deals had been asked about before.

**When you want an answer your history doesn't steer:** use a **temporary chat**, which leaves long-term memory out.

**To see what it has kept about you:** *"Can you create a caricature of me based on what you know about me?"*
